text: 7,10,11 The rate of major abnormality with phenytoin does not seem to be higher than in the general population.7 However, a well established fetal antiepileptic syndrome (FAS) has been reported with phenytoin, as with other antiepileptic drugs,6 including some older drugs such as trimethadione. Al- though early reports associated syndromes with specific drugs, such as fetal hydantoin syndrome (phenytoin), or fetal valproate syndrome, there is considerable overlap in the reported effects and recent reviews consider these as manifestations of a single condition, FAS.6,11 The dysmor- phic facial changes characteristic of FAS can be quite sub- tle, and may become less apparent as the child grows.7 Evidence for any effect of the newer antiepileptics on the fetus is particularly scanty. It is unclear if oxcarbazepine is associated with an increased risk in major malformation,7 and limited data have not so far suggested a significant in- crease in risk with lamotrigine11,19,21 and levetiracetam.22 There are reports suggestive of an increased risk with topiramate7 and licensed product information for this Antiepileptics 469 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) drug, and also pregabalin and zonisamide advises against use in pregnancy on the basis of animal studies and lack of human data. Caution is also advised with tiagabine and vi- gabatrin. There appears to be little evidence of teratogenic potential for felbamate or gabapentin in animal studies to date, although cases of malformation have been seen in pregnancies exposed to gabapentin.7 In a study23 of the UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register, which examined the outcome of 3607 pregnancies in mothers with epilepsy, the overall rate of major congenital malformations was 3.5% in those untreated with antiepi- leptics and 4.2% in those given antiepileptics during preg- nancy, with rates of 3.7% and 6.0% in those given mono- therapy or polytherapy respectively. For monotherapy the malformation rates for individual drugs were topiramate (7.1%), valproate (6.2%), phenytoin (3.7%), gabapentin (3.2%), lamotrigine (3.2%), and carbamazepine (2.2%). For polytherapy, those regimens containing valproate had a significantly higher risk of major congenital malforma- tions than valproate-free combinations. For monotherapy a relationship between malformations and dose was seen for lamotrigine and although the trend with valproate dos- age did not reach statistical significance infants exposed to more than 1000 mg valproate daily had the highest rate of malformations for any monotherapy.
